summary.text: A rain shadow is a much drier area behind a mountain range, on the leeward side that faces away from the prevailing winds.
Moist air forced up the windward slope expands and cools, so its moisture condenses and falls as precipitation before it crosses the top.
The air then sinks down the far side, warming as it is compressed, which lets it soak up moisture and leaves a dry region behind.

facts.label: Dry side name
facts.value: Leeward side, facing away from prevailing winds

facts.label: Wet side name
facts.value: Windward side, also called the rainward side

facts.label: Cape contrast
facts.value: About 1,500 mm on peaks versus 200 mm at Worcester

facts.label: Myanmar contrast
facts.value: About 750 mm inland versus up to 5.5 m on coast

items.prompt: Wet ocean winds blow steadily from the west onto a tall north–south mountain range. Where will the driest land likely be?

options.label: On the western slopes facing the ocean
Right on the highest peaks of the range
On the land east of the mountains
Along the coast west of the range

items.explain: Air loses most of its moisture going up the windward (western) side, so the leeward side, here the east, ends up in the rain shadow.

items.prompt: Why does moist air drop its water as it is pushed up a mountainside?

options.label: It expands and cools until moisture condenses
It warms up and the water boils out
It collides with rock that squeezes it dry
It speeds up and the water is flung out

items.explain: Rising air meets lower pressure, expands and cools to its dew point, so its moisture condenses and precipitates.

items.prompt: As air sinks down the dry side of a mountain range, what happens to it?

options.label: It cools and fills with fresh fog
It is compressed, warms, and dries the land
It slows down and drops heavy rain
It rises again and forms storm clouds

items.explain: Descending air is compressed and heated, which raises how much moisture it can absorb and creates an arid region.

items.prompt: A small mountain range is short and narrow. How would its rain shadow likely compare with that of a huge, wide range?

options.label: It would be far drier than the huge range's
It would be exactly as dry as the huge range's
It would move to the windward side instead
It would be weaker, as more moisture crosses

items.explain: Most humidity is lost before the crest only if the landforms are tall and wide enough, so a small range lets more moisture through.

items.prompt: Which kind of landscape would you most expect to find in a strong rain shadow?

options.label: Dense tropical rainforest
Shrublands or desert
Swamps and wide marshes
Thick mossy cloud forest

items.explain: Rain shadow climates typically take the form of shrub–steppe, xeric shrublands, or deserts.

items.prompt: Madagascar gets onshore winds from the east and has central highlands. Which side of the island ends up with thorn forests and deserts?

options.label: The eastern side, where the winds arrive
Only the central highland peaks
The northern tip, nearest the equator
The western and southern sides

items.explain: The windward east is wet tropical, while the western and southern sides lie in the rain shadow of the central highlands.

paragraphs.heading: What a rain shadow is
paragraphs.text: A rain shadow is an area behind a range of mountains where rainfall drops sharply. It lies on the leeward side, the side turned away from the prevailing winds. The dry land there usually becomes shrub–steppe, xeric shrubland or outright desert.

paragraphs.heading: Rising air drops its water
paragraphs.text: Winds blowing in from oceans and large lakes carry evaporated moisture toward drier, hotter land further inland. When that moist air meets mountains, it is pushed up the slope, a process called orographic lifting. As it climbs, air pressure falls, so the air expands and cools until it reaches its dew point, the point where its moisture condenses. The water then falls on the summit and the windward side, the side facing the wind. If the mountains are tall and wide enough, most of the moisture is lost this way before the air ever crosses the top.

paragraphs.heading: Sinking air dries the land
paragraphs.text: On the far side, the air comes down having already lost much of its water. As it descends it is squeezed and heats up, which lets it take up more moisture. This warm air, which can form what are called foehn winds, draws moisture from the slopes below and leaves a broad dry zone behind the peaks.

paragraphs.heading: Winds decide the dry side
paragraphs.text: The shadow falls on the side away from the prevailing winds, and those winds follow regular bands around the Earth. The trade winds, between about 30° N and 30° S, come mainly out of the northeast north of the equator and out of the southeast south of it. The westerlies, between 30 and 60 degrees of latitude, come mainly out of the southwest in the north and out of the northwest in the south.

paragraphs.heading: The Sahara and the Atlas
paragraphs.text: The Sahara is made even drier by the rain shadows of major mountain ranges. To its northwest, moist winds off the Atlantic run into the Atlas Mountains, are forced upward, cool, and drop heavy rain over the range. This is known as orographic rainfall, and the air leaves the mountains dry. Coming down the other side, it sinks, compresses and warms, so clouds evaporate, rain cannot form, and desert conditions follow.

paragraphs.heading: Shadows around the world
paragraphs.text: In South Africa's Western Cape, the Breede River Valley and the Karoo are dry, lying in the rain shadow cast by the Cape Fold Mountains. The wettest parts of the Cape Mountains can get 1,500 mm of rain a year, while Worcester gets only around 200 mm and is useful only for grazing. Central Myanmar, behind the Arakan Mountains, gets about 750 mm, against up to 5.5 metres on the Rakhine State coast. On Madagascar, the windward side that catches easterly winds from the sea is wet and tropical, while the western and southern sides hold thorn forests and deserts. Further north, the Himalayas and nearby ranges help make Central Asia dry, including Mongolia's Gobi Desert.
